segments.text: What's up guys, welcome back to CrimeTimeSnacks.
A college student crashed her car on a snowy New Hampshire road and vanished without a trace before police arrived.
It happened on February 9, 2004.
The student was Maura Murray, a twenty-one-year-old nursing major at UMass Amherst.
She was driving her black Saturn sedan that evening.
Sometime after seven o'clock, the car went off the road on a sharp corner on Route 112 in Haverhill, New Hampshire.
The vehicle ended up against a snowbank, pointing west on the eastbound side of the road.
A local resident heard a loud thump outside her house.
The resident looked out her window and saw the car.
She called the sheriff's department at 7:27 p.m. to report the accident.
The 911 log shows the woman initially claimed to see a man smoking a cigarette inside the car.
She later changed her statement, saying she actually saw a red light glowing from inside, possibly from a cell phone.
Right around that time, a school bus driver who lived nearby passed the scene.
He stopped and saw a young woman walking around the Saturn.
He noticed she was cold and shivering, but not bleeding or visibly injured.
He offered to call for help.
The woman asked him not to call the police.
She assured him she had already called AAA, even though AAA has no record of that call.
The bus driver knew there was no cellular reception in the area.
He drove the rest of the way home and called the police himself.
The sheriff's department received his call at 7:43 p.m. While making the call from his house, he could not see the crash site, but he noticed several cars pass by on the road.
The official police log states a Haverhill officer arrived at the scene at 7:46 p.m. The female driver was gone.
There is a conflicting account about that arrival time.
Another local resident driving home from work claimed she passed the scene around 7:37 p.m. She said she saw a police SUV parked face-to-face with Maura's car.
She pulled over briefly, saw nobody around either vehicle, and continued home.
Whenever the first officer actually arrived, they found the Saturn locked and severely damaged.
The left headlight was smashed and the radiator was pushed into the fan.
Both airbags had deployed.
Inside and outside the car, the officer found red stains that looked like red wine.
The police found an empty beer bottle and a damaged box of wine on the rear seat.
They also found a AAA card, blank accident report forms, makeup, diamond jewelry, and driving directions to Burlington.
Maura's debit card, credit cards, and cell phone were missing.
She has not been seen since.
To understand how she got there, we have to start at the beginning.
The record shows Maura was born on May 4, 1982.
Her hometown was Brockton, Massachusetts.
She was the fourth child of Fred and Laurie Murray.
The family raised their children in a traditional Irish Catholic household.
Her parents divorced when Maura was just six years old.
After the split, she lived primarily with her mother.
She grew up in a busy house alongside her older brother Fred, her older sisters Kathleen and Julie, and her younger half-brother Kurt.
By the time she reached high school, Maura was making a name for herself.
She attended Whitman-Hanson Regional High School in Hanson, Massachusetts.
What the evidence actually shows is a highly driven teenager.
She became a star athlete on the school's track team.
That athletic and academic drive paid off in a major way.
Maura was accepted into the United States Military Academy in West Point, New York.
She enrolled and spent three semesters studying chemical engineering.
It was an incredibly demanding program.
But her time at the academy did not end with a degree.
During a training period at Fort Knox, Maura was accused of stealing from the base exchange.
Some early news accounts claimed she was on the verge of being expelled for the theft.
Her sister Julie later clarified what actually happened with the military leadership.
The theft allegation was officially referred to a West Point honor board.
Julie stated that even if the board found the accusation to be true, the punishment would not have been outright expulsion.
Maura never waited around to find out what the honor board would decide.
Believing West Point was simply not a good fit for her anymore, she made a major life change.
She chose on her own to leave the military academy before the board ever convened.
After her freshman year, she transferred to the University of Massachusetts Amherst.
She changed her academic focus completely and began studying nursing.
But trouble seemed to follow her to the new campus.
In November 2003, just three months before she vanished, Maura found herself in legal trouble again.
She admitted to using a stolen credit card to order food from several local restaurants.
The court continued the charge in December.
It was scheduled to be dismissed after three months of good behavior.
That credit card incident wasn't the only weight on her shoulders that winter.
On the evening of Thursday, February 5, 2004, Maura was working her security job on the UMass Amherst campus.
While on duty, she talked on the phone with her older sister, Kathleen.
They discussed Kathleen's relationship problems with her fiancé.
The exact details of that call stayed private for years.
In 2017, Kathleen publicly explained what happened that night.
Kathleen had just been discharged from a rehabilitation clinic.
On the way home, her fiancé took her to a liquor store, causing a relapse.
Around 10:30 p.m., still on her shift, Maura reportedly broke down in tears.
When her supervisor checked on her, Maura was completely zoned out and unresponsive.
The supervisor ended up escorting her back to her dorm room around 1:20 in the morning.
When asked what was wrong, Maura just said two words.
She said, "My sister."
Two days later, on Saturday, February 7, her father Fred came to town.
He told investigators they went car shopping that afternoon.
Later, they grabbed dinner with one of Maura's friends.
After dinner, Maura dropped her dad off at his motel room.
She borrowed his Toyota Corolla and headed back to campus for a dorm party.
The timeline shows she got there around 10:30 p.m. and stayed until 2:30 Sunday morning.
On her way back to her father's motel at 3:30 a.m., she struck a guardrail on Route 9 in Hadley.
The crash caused nearly ten thousand dollars in damage to her dad's car.
A responding officer wrote up an accident report.
The case file shows no documentation of any field sobriety tests being conducted.
Maura was driven to the motel and stayed in her father's room for the rest of the morning.
At 4:49 a.m., a call went out from Fred's cell phone to Maura's boyfriend.
We still do not know exactly who made that call or what was said.
Later that morning, Fred found out his auto insurance would cover the damage to the Corolla.
He rented a car, dropped Maura back at campus, and headed for Connecticut.
That Sunday night at 11:30, Fred called his daughter.
He wanted to remind her to get the official accident forms from the Massachusetts Registry of Motor Vehicles.
They agreed to talk again Monday night to fill out the insurance claim over the phone.
You already know about the legal trouble hanging over her head.
The court had just continued that charge in December.
Now she was dealing with a wrecked car on top of it.
Shortly after midnight on Monday, February 9, she got on her personal computer.
She searched MapQuest for directions to the Berkshires and Burlington, Vermont.
Classes at UMass Amherst were canceled that day because of a snowstorm.
At 1:00 p.m., Maura emailed her boyfriend.
She told him she had received his messages but didn't feel like talking to anyone.
She promised to call him later that day.
Then she started making phone calls.
She called a number about renting a condominium in Bartlett, New Hampshire.
Her family had vacationed there in the past.
The call lasted three minutes.
The owner later said they did not rent to her and could not even remember speaking with her.
At 1:13 p.m., she called a fellow nursing student.
The reason for that call is still unknown.
Private investigator John Healey suggested she may have arranged to give her scrubs to a fellow student, while a family member posited she might have been returning borrowed scrubs.
At 1:24 p.m., she sent an email to a nursing school faculty supervisor.
She wrote that she would be out of town for a week because of a death in her family.
She promised to contact them when she got back.
Her family later confirmed there was no death.
Just after two o'clock, she dialed a recorded information line for booking hotels in Stowe, Vermont.
That call lasted about five minutes.
At 2:18 p.m., she left a one-minute voicemail for her boyfriend, promising again to talk later.
In her dorm room, Maura was packing.
She loaded her car with clothing, toiletries, textbooks, and birth control pills.
When campus police eventually searched her room, they found her art taken off the walls and most of her belongings packed in boxes.
Police believe she packed those boxes between Sunday night and Monday morning.
On top of them, she left a printed email to her boyfriend that hinted at relationship trouble.
Around 3:30 p.m., she drove off campus.
Ten minutes later, security cameras recorded her alone at an ATM.
She withdrew two hundred and eighty dollars.
She then went to a nearby liquor store.
Footage shows she was alone there, too.
She bought about forty dollars' worth of alcohol, including vodka, Baileys, Kahlúa, and that box of Franzia wine found in her car.
At some point that day, she also picked up the official accident forms.
Between four and five o'clock, she left Amherst.
Think back to that security shift on February 5.
That happened after talking to her sister Kathleen about that recent relapse.
Her supervisor found her completely zoned out at her desk.
She was entirely unresponsive.
That breakdown at work is the lens investigators used to view everything that followed.
She was carrying the weight of her sister's struggle, her own pending credit card charge, and a wrecked borrowed car.
As she drove away from Amherst that Monday afternoon, she made one final move.
At 4:37 p.m., she called to check her voicemail.
The record shows that was the last recorded use of her cell phone.
The case file shows no indication she told a single person where she was going.
There is no evidence she had even chosen a final destination.
The next day, February 10, the search officially started.
At 12:36 p.m., police issued a 'be on the lookout' report for Maura.
They listed her as wearing a dark coat, jeans, and a black backpack.
At 3:20 p.m., someone left a voicemail on her father Fred's home answering machine.
The message stated her car had been found abandoned.
But Fred was working out of state and never got that call.
At five o'clock that evening, one of Maura's older sisters finally reached Fred to tell him what was going on.
He immediately contacted the Haverhill police.
The department told him that if Maura was not reported safe by the following morning, the New Hampshire Fish and Game Department would step in.
Seventeen minutes later, at 5:17 p.m., Haverhill police officially referred to Maura as missing.
Fred arrived in Haverhill before dawn on February 11.
At eight o'clock that morning, the physical search finally began.
The New Hampshire Fish and Game Department brought in a tracking dog.
The dog picked up Maura's scent from one of her gloves.
The trail went exactly one hundred yards east from where the Saturn was found.
Then the scent just vanished.
Investigators suggested this meant she got into another vehicle and left the area.
Around that time, Maura's boyfriend and his parents arrived in town.
Police interrogated the boyfriend in private before bringing his parents in for questioning.
Two hours later, investigators announced their working theory.
They believed Maura came to the area to either run away or attempt suicide.
Her family pushed back immediately, calling that highly unlikely.
But the police doubled down.
The next day, February 12, they issued a report stating she might be headed to the Kancamagus Highway area.
They listed her as endangered and possibly suicidal.
The official police report also stated she was intoxicated at the crash site.
That directly contradicted the bus driver, who had told them she did not appear impaired.
There was one more strange detail from those early days.
The boyfriend had turned off his cell phone during his flight to Haverhill.
When he checked his messages, he found a voicemail that he believed was the sound of Maura sobbing.
Police traced the call, but it only led back to a calling card issued to the American Red Cross.
He told investigators they spent the afternoon car shopping.
The timeline shows she got there around 10:30 p.m. and stayed until 2:30 Sunday morning.
The case file shows no documentation of any field sobriety tests being conducted.
We still do not know exactly who made that call or what was said.
That night at 11:30, Fred called his daughter.
The case file does not show who actually dialed the number or what they talked about.
Later that morning, the immediate situation with the wrecked car was resolved.
Later that Sunday, Fred rented a car, dropped Maura back at UMass Amherst, and left for Connecticut.
The 11:30 call was about accident forms from the Registry of Motor Vehicles, and they agreed to talk again Monday night.
The first reported contact she had with anyone on Monday, February 9, came at 1:00 p.m., when she sent an email to her boyfriend.
We have the exact message she typed out.
She wrote, "I love you more stud.
I got your messages, but honestly, I didn't feel like talking too much of anyone, I promise to call today though.
Love you, Maura."
Right after sending that email, she picked up the phone.
You remember that three-minute call.
Telephone records confirm the exact length of that call, even though the owner never ended up renting to her.
You already know she lied to get off campus.
That email was completely fabricated.
Her relatives were clear with investigators later.
Nobody had died.
She was creating a cover story.
It was a deliberate choice to buy herself time and keep the school from looking for her.
Right before sending that fake excuse, she made that 1:13 p.m. call to a fellow nursing student.
The case file shows a family member, Helena Murray, also thought the same thing.
Helena posited that Maura was just trying to give back a borrowed uniform before leaving.
Whatever the real reason, she was tying up loose ends.
She was clearing the decks.
She had her fake excuse in place and her car loaded for a trip north.
Now let's look at how the investigation actually evolved over the years.
The local police initially treated this as a voluntary disappearance.
They pointed to her packed dorm room and that fake family death email as proof she wanted to walk away.
But that stance eventually shifted.
In 2009, the case was officially transferred to the New Hampshire cold case unit.
The record shows they now classify it as a suspicious missing-person investigation.
Investigators have not just been sitting on the original case file.
They have actively searched for physical evidence in the area around the crash.
In 2019, law enforcement announced a major update.
They went back to a specific house in Haverhill.
They had searched the property years earlier, but they had never actually looked inside the dwelling.
This time, they brought in specialized tools.
They used local dogs and a ground-penetrating radar scan in the basement.
The radar data seemed to indicate the ground under the house had been moved at some point.
Police actually dug up the basement floor looking for Maura.
But the search came up empty.
They found no new clues about what happened to her.
State prosecutors and police also recently went back to two neighboring New Hampshire towns.
They returned to Landaff and Easton to conduct a more extensive search of areas that were only briefly checked back in 2004.
They are still looking for any physical trace.
There was also a development involving forensic evidence from the Saturn.
A detective named Charles West found a fingerprint match.
He contacted police in Ohio to report that prints found in Maura's car matched a troubled West Point cadet named Steffen.
At the time, the detective called this man his number one suspect.
Through all of this, Maura's family has pushed back hard against the original police theory.
Her sister Julie has been incredibly vocal.
By 2025, she even launched her own podcast to reclaim the narrative.
The family believes Maura most likely met with foul play after leaving the crash scene.
They are frustrated by the early missed opportunities and the incomplete communication from law enforcement.
They believe too much time was lost to competing theories before the surviving evidence was re-examined with modern tools.
To understand why police initially clung to that runaway theory, we have to look back at her dorm room.
But what she left behind tells its own story.
When campus police finally unlocked her door, it did not look like the room of someone just taking a few days off.
The walls were completely bare.
All of her art had been taken down.
Almost everything she owned was packed away in boxes.
One early report even mentioned she left a note for her roommates.
Friends later reported she had been acting strangely in the days leading up to her disappearance.
They told investigators she was under immense stress due to school and personal issues.
That context made the packed room look even more like a deliberate, permanent exit.
Then there was the printed email.
She left it sitting right on top of those packed boxes.
It was a message to her boyfriend, and it clearly indicated they were having relationship trouble.
That single printed page sitting on a stack of boxes shaped the entire early investigation.
You do not box up your life and leave a troubled email on top if you plan on coming back to school.
At least, that is what the local police argued.
The runaway theory also relied heavily on what investigators found inside the wrecked Saturn.
When that Haverhill officer looked through the locked car, he found more than just the deployed airbags and the smashed radiator.
He noted the windshield was cracked on the driver's side.
The officer inventoried the personal items left behind in the cold.
He found her favorite stuffed animal sitting in the vehicle.
He also found her compact discs and her gloves.
There was one specific item that really caught their attention.
Police found a book titled Not Without Peril.
It is a book entirely about mountain climbing in the White Mountains.
Finding that specific book in the car made police even more certain she had headed north on purpose.
But not everything she brought with her was still in the car.
The police later reported that some of the bottles of liquor she purchased back in Amherst were also gone.
The combination of the abandoned car, the packed room, and the missing items turned this into a massive story.
Over the years, the case has been featured on ABC's 20/20, the Oxygen Channel, and Montel Williams.
It has been covered by Dr. Oz, E!
News, and People magazine.
A journalist named Joe McGee summarized the sheer baffling nature of the scene for a Massachusetts newspaper.
He wrote that she went off the road at a hairpin turn and hit a tree.
He noted that a neighbor driving a bus offered help, which she refused.
McGee wrote that about ten minutes later, police showed up to the scene and Maura Murray was gone.
She drove her black 1996 Saturn sedan away around 3:30 p.m. that Monday.
The snowstorm had canceled her classes, giving her a clear window to leave.
The FBI later noted that the roads in that specific area of northern New Hampshire were completely snow-covered at the time.
We tracked her to the ATM where she pulled out two hundred and eighty dollars.
We know she spent about forty dollars on alcohol right after that.
That left her with a decent amount of cash to travel with as she made her way out of Massachusetts.
With her car loaded, investigators presume she headed up Interstate 91 North.
At 4:37 p.m., she dialed in to check her voicemail.
The timeline of this drive is crucial because it sets up the boundary for everything that followed.
What the evidence actually shows is that this was the final recorded use of her cell phone.
She drove into a rural landscape where cellular reception was practically non-existent.
From there, she drove toward Woodsville, a small village in the town of Haverhill.
The Oxygen documentary series later called her case one of the first major crime mysteries of the early social media era.
That digital era is a big reason why this case has stayed so visible.
True crime enthusiasts have spent nearly two decades debating what actually happened on that route.
Some theories point directly to mental health struggles.
Proponents of this idea argue the stress and anxiety she was experiencing could have led her to run away or harm herself.
Other people look at the geography of northern New Hampshire.
They suggest she might have encountered an accident in a remote area, becoming lost or injured in the wilderness without anyone knowing.
Her disappearance eventually made international headlines.
Beyond the shows we already talked about, her story was covered by the program Disappeared, the Daily Mail, and the New York Daily News.
It became one of the most followed missing persons cases in the world.
The sheer volume of attention pushed authorities to keep looking.
Cold case teams have recently looked back at her digital footprint from those final hours.
They are still trying to match potential sightings reported along her route with the timeline of that drive.
Investigators are applying new technology to the old evidence.
They are using advanced search techniques and modern forensic tools to review the files.
They want to find any missing piece that could finally explain where she went.
You already know this case was profiled on national programs like 20/20 and Disappeared.
I mentioned that Oxygen documentary.
That timing is exactly why the public reaction became its own strange chapter in this story.
When Maura vanished, the social web was just being born.
Facebook was exactly five days old.
There was no Twitter and no YouTube, but the internet caught up fast.
By 2005, active discussions about the crash were taking over message boards.
Two years later, dedicated social media pages were popping up everywhere.
The case became a total obsession for amateur sleuths.
People started dissecting every single detail from the official timeline with what one writer called a Warren Commission-like fervor.
They treated her disappearance like a puzzle.
The internet offered this tantalizing illusion that if someone just connected the right dots online, they could solve the unsolvable.
But this is not a victory lap for online sleuths.
A lot of that public reaction was completely unhelpful.
It generated years of noise and misinformation that actively frustrated the actual investigation.
Strangers online started pushing elaborate theories as absolute fact.
One prominent argument claimed she traveled into New Hampshire with a tandem driver.
The theory suggested she willingly started a new life somewhere else to escape that pending credit card charge.
Author James Renner proposed she was murdered by someone she knew.
Her family had to read all of this speculation while living through a nightmare.
They strongly disputed the idea that she ran away to start over.
Her father maintained his belief that his daughter was abducted and is dead.
But the internet kept spinning its own narratives anyway, forcing the family to combat the rumors.
They were forced to stop being passive observers.
That was a direct response to this online circus.
Her relatives spent years trying to cut through the noise because they wanted the public to focus on the actual physical evidence.
They needed people to recognize that Maura likely left the crash area in circumstances that were far more dangerous than the internet wanted to admit.
The digital footprint of this case remains a double-edged sword.
Viral posts occasionally prompted new witnesses to come forward with tips, but it also meant her loved ones had to constantly fight to reclaim her story from the internet.
You already know the local police initially thought Maura walked away voluntarily.
You also know that stance shifted when the unit officially labeled it a suspicious disappearance.
Since that transfer, the case file shows a relentless push for answers.
Back in 2006 and 2008, licensed private investigators and dog teams combed the wooded areas around Haverhill.
An Arkansas group even put up a seventy-five-thousand-dollar reward to generate new information.
Her father Fred publicly criticized the early investigation in 2010.
He argued it should have been treated as a criminal matter from day one, and he called on the FBI to join the search.
The FBI eventually did step up, issuing a national alert in 2022 and adding the case to their Violent Criminal Apprehension Profile.
In 2024, marking exactly twenty years since the crash, officials released an updated age-progression photo.
The unit issued a statement in 2026.
They confirmed they still work with federal partners daily to pursue every credible lead.
But despite multiple searches and massive public appeals, the record is stark.
No confirmed sightings have ever emerged in over two decades.
Not a single definitive lead has pointed to exactly where she went after the bus driver drove away.
Even promising physical traces have led nowhere.
In the fall of 2021, state police announced that bone fragments were found on Loon Mountain.
That is about twenty-five miles east of the crash site.
Maura's sister noted she had been to that mountain before and knew the area.
Investigators warned the fragments were small and would take time to test.
Two months later, they announced the remains did not belong to Maura.
It was just another dead end in a case full of them.
That same year, the property owner cut down the tree where Maura was last seen.
The state also denied the family's request to place a historical marker at the site.
The physical reminders of that night are slowly fading from Route 112.
We are left with an abandoned Saturn, locked, with a cracked windshield.
The facts end at that snowbank in Haverhill.
Read the file.
Form your own conclusion.
That's it for this one.
Thanks for hanging out with me.
This has been CrimeTimeSnacks, and I'll catch you next time.
